vignette:
He is 29, a South Asian man who makes his living as a painter, the kind of person who is used to steady work with his hands. Before the robbery, his days are simple and physical. He wakes early, drinks tea with his wife, loads drop cloths and paint cans into the van, and spends long hours on ladders cutting careful lines along ceilings or rolling color across walls. He likes the quiet satisfaction of finishing a room and stepping back to see it transformed. He is not especially talkative, but at home he jokes easily, calls his mother often, and takes pride in sending money when family needs help. He thinks of himself as practical, someone who manages what is in front of him.

The robbery happens on an ordinary weeknight, which is part of what stays with him. He has finished a small job later than expected and stops on the way home to pick up dinner. In the parking lot, while he is unlocking the van, two men come up behind him. At first he thinks they are asking for directions. Then one of them grabs his shoulder hard enough to spin him around, and the other presses something cold into his side. Even now, he is not fully sure whether it is a knife or a gun, only that his body understands danger before his mind catches up. They demand his wallet, his phone, the keys. One man curses at him when his hands shake and he fumbles in his pocket. He remembers the smell of sweat and cigarettes, the scrape of asphalt under his work boots, the sudden strange thought that he should not get paint on the food container still in his hand. When one of them shoves him to the ground, he feels a bright burst of pain in his elbow and cheek. He lies still after they run, listening to his own breathing and the fading sound of the van pulling away.

In the hours after, he is embarrassed almost as much as he is frightened. He calls his wife from a stranger's phone and hears his own voice sounding thin and unfamiliar. At the police station he gives his statement, but details slip away or return in flashes that seem too vivid. He goes home sore and exhausted, expecting sleep to come from sheer depletion. Instead he lies awake replaying the moment he turned and saw them. Each time he starts to drift, he jerks himself back, his heart pounding as if someone is in the room.

In the weeks that follow, he tells people he is "fine," but his life grows narrower. He no longer wants to work evening jobs, then starts refusing jobs in certain neighborhoods, then avoids stopping anywhere alone after dark. He asks his wife to come with him on errands and becomes irritated when she points out that she has her own work. He begins checking locks repeatedly before bed and looking out the apartment window whenever he hears a car slow down outside. If someone approaches him unexpectedly, his shoulders tense and his whole body turns before he can think. On job sites, the drop of a tool or a voice behind him makes him flinch so sharply that coworkers laugh, then stop laughing when they see his face.

The worst part for him is how the robbery enters the places that once felt most familiar. He is on a ladder edging trim when he suddenly sees, as clearly as if it is happening again, a hand lunging toward his shoulder. Paint drips down the wall while he freezes, brush suspended in the air. Sometimes he has to go sit in the van, sweating, waiting for the feeling to pass. He starts taking longer to finish jobs because he keeps scanning driveways, watching passing strangers, calculating where he would run. Customers notice that he seems distracted. A contractor he works with regularly tells him he is making careless mistakes, and he feels ashamed because carefulness has always been part of his identity.

At home, his wife says he is present in body but not really with her. He snaps when she asks harmless questions like what time he will be back or whether he picked up groceries. Then he feels guilty and withdraws further. Physical closeness becomes difficult; if she reaches for him when he is half asleep, he startles violently and sometimes pushes her away before he knows who she is. He hates the look on her face afterward. He begins staying up late with the television on, not really watching, because going to sleep means risking the same dream: the parking lot, the command to hand things over, the certainty that one wrong move will end his life.

He tells himself he should be over it. Other people have had worse happen. He was not killed, not even badly injured. Yet months later he still plans his routes to avoid that street. He keeps seeing men who resemble the attackers in every gas station and store aisle. He holds his breath when strangers stand too close behind him. He misses the version of himself who could move through the day without calculating danger, who could finish a job and go home tired in the ordinary way. Now even when a room is freshly painted and perfect, he does not feel the old satisfaction for long. Relief comes in short bursts, quickly replaced by the sense that something can be taken from him again at any moment.
